It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and its former {{ill|Shakaku|ja|社格|ko|사격 (신토)|zh|社格|qid=Q10444029}} was {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}. {{nihongo|'''Hokura Shrine'''|保久良神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Settsu Province]].

It enshrines {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|qid=Q272993}}, {{ill|Ōkuninushi|lt=Ōkuninushi-no-Mikoto|qid=Q276944}}, {{ill|Toshigami|fr|Toshigami|it|Toshigami|ja|年神|mni|ꯇꯣꯁꯤꯒꯃꯤ|pl|Toshigami|ru|Тосигами|simple|Toshigami|uk|Тосіґамі|zh|年神|qid=Q3028663|lt=Ōtoshi-mioya-no-Mikoto}}, and {{ill|Saonetsuhiko|fr|Saonetsuhiko|ja|椎根津彦|zh|槁根津彥|qid=Q11120574|lt=Shiine-tsuhiko-no-Mikoto}}.

==History==
Details of the foundation are unknown, but many groups of {{ill|Iwakura rock|Q11587880|qid=Q11587880}} inside and outside the precinct suggest an ancient ritual site. Various relics from the Stone Age, Bronze Age, and late Yayoi period have been excavated from inside and outside the shrine grounds, including Yayoi pottery, stone axes, and stone swords; most famous is a c.20 cm bronze halberd (Important Cultural Property). All are considered ritual-use objects. ''Hafuri'' pottery and glass magatama were also found, indicating worship from very early times<ref name="#1">''Shrines of Kobe: Guide to 310 shrines in the city'', 2000, Kobe branch of Hyōgo Prefecture Shrine Office.</ref>.

According to the shrine history, the shrine name derives either from (1) descendants of Shiine-tsuhiko-no-Mikoto, such as Kurabito Mizumori, worshiping their ancestor, or (2) storing captured weapons from the campaign against the Three Han. The original main deity was Shiine-tsuhiko-no-Mikoto, who appeared at {{ill|Hayasui-no-to|ja|速吸門|qid=Q11639656}} ({{ill|Akashi Strait|Q845336|qid=Q845336}}) during {{ill|Jimmu's Eastern Expedition|fa|اردوکشی شرقی جینمو|fr|Expédition orientale de Jimmu|ja|神武東征|ko|진무 동정|zh|神武東征|qid=Q11590444}} and led the army<ref>''Historical Walks of Hyōgo Prefecture, Upper Volume: Kobe/Hanshin/Awaji'', 2006, Yamakawa Shuppansha.</ref>.

A legend says Shiine-tsuhiko arrived at Ōgi beach in {{ill|Ōgi|Q11661589|qid=Q11661589|lt=Ōgi}}, south of Hokura Shrine, riding on the back of a blue turtle (ōgi), and that this became the origin of the place name Ōgi<ref name="#1"/>.

Yoshii Yoshitaka inferred that this shrine was originally Oku-ebi-sha of Nishinomiya Ebisu, with Shiine-tsuhiko as chief of the maritime people controlling the north side of Osaka Bay<ref>''Gods of Japan - Shrines and Sacred Places - 3 Settsu/Kawachi/Izumi/Awaji'', 2000, ed. Tanigawa Kenichi et al., Hakusuisha.</ref>. The "Sumiyoshi Taisha shrine records" mention the name Fukurofu-yama, and ''Settsushi'' records possession of a ridge tag from a major repair in Kenchō 2.

The sacred fire at the shrine’s light platform is the eternal lamp called "Nada no hitotsubi." Tradition says that when {{ill|Yamato Takeru|lt=Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258}} lost his route at sea at night while returning from the {{ill|Kumaso|Q1196897|qid=Q1196897}} expedition, he saw the light of Hokura Shrine and safely returned to Naniwa. Since then, as in the old song, "for boats offshore, a guide to rely on, the single light of Nada," it was widely revered as a maritime guide<ref name="#1"/>.

==Festivals==
* January 20 - Ōdawara Festival
* May 4-5 - Annual grand festival
* July 14 - Nagoshi Festival
* August 11 - Ancestor-deity festival

==Around the shrine==
West of Hokura Shrine is Hokura Plum Grove, planted in 1975 (Shōwa 50), with about 150 white-plum trees and about 100 red-plum trees including Shirakaga and Maya-kōbai<ref>[https://www.city.kobe.lg.jp/b07715/kuyakusho/higashinadaku/shoukai/shoukai/ume.html Kobe City website: Higashinada highlights - plum blossoms]</ref>.
Also between this shrine and the plum grove runs a hiking trail from {{ill|Kinchōzan|ja|金鳥山|qid=Q97658192}} via {{ill|Kaze-fuki-iwa|Q97674252|qid=Q97674252}} to the highest peak of {{ill|Mount Rokkō|Q462120|qid=Q462120}}. Because it is close to the urban area, like {{ill|Mount Futatabi|Q11394928|qid=Q11394928}}, {{ill|Takatori mountain|Q11668943|qid=Q11668943}}, and Hatafuri-yama, “daily climbing” is popular and many climbers have exceeded 1,000 ascents.

On the southern {{ill|Fault scarp|Q475080|qid=Q475080}} where the zigzag approach path runs up to the shrine, slope countermeasure works commissioned by the {{ill|Rokko Sabo Office|Q18457447|qid=Q18457447}} have been conducted since 2016, including frame and anchor works to reduce {{ill|slide|Q3574985|qid=Q3574985|lt=collapse on steep slopes}}.
